Finland plans anti-tank barriers on Russian border as Moscow rearms

Finland is reviewing Ukraine-style defences and strengthening its military, which can mobilise 280,000 troops in wartime, to deter a Russian attack.

Kirsi Heikel

07 November, 2026 09:36 pm IST

Finland is studying Ukraine-style anti-tank obstacles to bolster its border with Russia as it works to strengthen defenses on NATO’s eastern flank against a rapidly rearming foe.

Lieutenant General Pasi Välimäki, commander of the Finnish Army, said in an interview that Russia had already begun rebuilding its military capacity, even as its full-scale invasion of Ukraine grinds into a fifth year.

In that conflict, Kyiv’s forces have used extensive defensive lines and anti-tank obstacles to slow attackers. Neither side has found a reliable way to break through them and restore large-scale movement and maneuver, Välimäki said.

Show Full Article

Sharing a 1,340-kilometer (830-mile) border with Russia, accounting for about half of NATO’s land frontier with that country, Finland must determine how structures similar to those used in Ukraine would fare in harsh northern weather.

“Conditions in Finland are more challenging,” Välimäki said. “If we build fortifications and dig anti-tank ditches or obstacles as deep as those in Ukraine, how long does it take before our environment turns them into artificial ponds?”

Russia’s efforts to replenish its weapons stockpiles are starting to show some effects, he said, with T-90 tanks, BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles and 2S19 self-propelled howitzers being delivered to storage sites.

Finland lacks the capacity to prevent that rearming. Rather, the goal is to deter Russia by convincing its military that an attack would fail, he said.

“Everything we are doing now is about creating a threshold so that Russia does not go any further, whether we are talking about the alliance or Finland,” Välimäki said.

Finland continued conscription and maintained territorial defense reserves after the Cold War, even as many European nations reduced their forces. Despite a population of just 5.6 million, its military can call on about 280,000 troops in wartime.

“When the war in Ukraine began, we improved our readiness and put 60,000 people through refresher training over two years,” Välimäki said. “We also quickly began replenishing stocks of critical materiel.”

Finland is now carrying out an overhaul of its land forces that will run through the end of the 2030s, covering equipment, force structure, readiness and the capacity to sustain combat. The basic approach — deterring an attack by being prepared — hasn’t changed, Välimäki said. What has changed is the scale required.

“The scale of the ammunition, production systems and trained personnel that we need to have ready for use is different from what it was before 2022,” he said. “It has to be larger, more sustainable and technologically more advanced than before.”

Finland will spend at least as much on the overhaul of its land forces as on its ongoing strategic Navy and Air Force programs combined, the Defense Ministry said in a written statement. Those programs have total funding of €11.6 billion ($13 billion).

As part of a much broader procurement drive, Finland is expanding its Hanwha Aerospace Co. Ltd. K9 self-propelled howitzer fleet, modernizing its heavy multiple-launch rocket systems to fire almost 500 kilometers, and preparing to replace its BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles.

Attacks on Ukraine have shown the scale of the air and missile threat Finland may face. Under the alliance’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Line concept, it isn’t enough to shoot down incoming missiles and drones — defenders must also be able to strike the launchers before they fire, Välimäki said.

“For Finns, this is a difficult issue, because it means hitting targets on the Russian side,” he said.

Finland has already begun replacing its F/A-18 Hornets with 64 Lockheed Martin Corp. F-35A fighters, with the first aircraft delivered. It has also ordered Israel’s David’s Sling missile-defense system, produced by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems Ltd., which has seen extensive action in the Iran war.

Välimäki rejects the idea that new technology has made traditional weapons obsolete. Drones have become a major part of the battlefield, Välimäki said, adding that they are only one element to consider.

Ukraine has also underscored the need to replenish equipment and ammunition during a prolonged conflict, and Välimäki wants domestic production that can expand rapidly.

“What I would like Finland to have is the ability to scale for mass-production in large volumes — production for readiness and daily training consumption that can be maintained in peacetime and scaled up tenfold in crisis and conflict,” he said.

The push reflects a fundamental constraint on how Finland can fight a much larger opponent on the eastern flank of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

“We do not want a war of attrition,” Välimäki said. “We are a country of five million people, and we cannot operate on that logic.”

Cyberattack at Russian stats agency Rosstat delays major economic reports

Rosstat failed to publish two scheduled weekly price releases as scheduled Friday, postponing them repeatedly before finally issuing the data. Some previously published information is also absent from the Rosstat website.

Bloomberg News

07 November, 2026 09:31 pm IST

Major Russian economic reports will be delayed through at least Nov. 13 following a recent major hack on the statistics agency Rosstat.

Rosstat failed to publish two scheduled weekly price releases as scheduled on Friday, postponing them repeatedly before finally issuing the data. Some previously published information is also absent from the Rosstat website.

The agency said it’s continuing to restore systems after a cyberattack knocked parts of its infrastructure offline, without providing more detail.

Show Full Article

“To ensure data security, some parts of the infrastructure remain isolated. This is necessary to allow thorough checks and a phased restoration of access,” the agency said on Thursday. “As a result, some website functions and parts of the IT infrastructure may be temporarily unavailable.”

While its website has resumed operating, deadlines for companies to submit statistical reports have been extended through Nov. 13. The longer collection period may result in further delays to individual data releases, the agency said.

The Belarusian pro-opposition group Cyber Partisans and the hacker operation Silent Crow claimed on Nov. 1 that they’d breached Rosstat’s internal infrastructure, gaining access to about 25,000 computers and extracting some 23 terabytes of data, including information on Russian military losses in the war against Ukraine.

Rosstat said that targeted cyberattacks on its systems were detected between Oct. 29 and Nov. 1, but that it found no evidence its databases had been compromised or confidential information leaked.

Since President Vladimir Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Kremlin has steadily restricted public access to official data, withholding or classifying an expanding range of information, including many economic and demographic indicators.

New Zealand election first count ends with two main parties nearly deadlocked

By Lucy Craymer and Alasdair Pal WELLINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) – New Zealand’s ruling centre-right National Party and main opposition Labour were nearly deadlocked in the popular vote after initial counting in the nationwide general election on Saturday.

Results from the Electoral Commission show that with more than 95% of the ballots counted, both parties were polling just short of 30% of the popular vote, with just a few thousand votes separating the two.

A projection from New Zealand’s Electoral Commission showed the current three-party ruling coalition led by National would have a majority of two seats, after an election dominated by a struggling economy and voter disillusionment with the two biggest contenders.

Show Full Article

Both parties said it would take time for the final results to be known.

“It is heartening to see that on the numbers so far, National is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government,” Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told supporters in Auckland.

“But I have to tell you right now, it is too close to call.”

Labour leader Chris Hipkins delivered a similar message in Upper Hutt, a city northeast of the capital Wellington.

“Tonight, New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said,” he told supporters.

GOVERNMENT COULD TAKE WEEKS

Special votes, which include those from overseas voters or people outside their electorate, will not be included in the vote count until official results are released on November 27.

Those votes have typically favoured the left, with parties on the right losing support following the count. This could also be key in seats where races remain tight between Labour and National candidates.

Left-leaning parties including Labour are aiming to make the National-led coalition the first one-term government in just over 50 years.

New Zealand’s electoral system makes coalitions the norm, and the tightness of this year’s race means one or more of the country’s smaller parties will almost certainly participate in a governing coalition.

The country switched to a mixed member proportional system in 1996, which means people vote for both the party and a local constituency candidate.

There are 71 constituency seats and at least 49 party seats, and a party or coalition needs a majority to form a government.

MINOR PARTIES WILL BE KEY

Popular support for Labour and National is at historically low levels, with surveys showing voters have lost faith in the major parties to find solutions to the sluggish economy and to make the necessary changes to fix ageing infrastructure.

If the National-led coalition loses its majority at the official count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would require the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, which looks likely to enter parliament for the first time.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said she would look to negotiate with the party that secured the largest number of seats after the official results.

“We made that call based on the fact that we need a majority of seats in parliament in order to form a government. So that is what we will stick to,” she told public broadcaster TVNZ.

New Zealand has emerged only slowly from a prolonged economic downturn, with growth subdued, household budgets strained and unemployment rising to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest level in 11 years.

Healthcare and hospitals rank alongside the economy as leading concerns for voters, while housing affordability is still a major issue, even though house prices have broadly stabilised.

Indigenous Maori voters are also concerned about the current government’s attempts to roll back historic policies meant to improve conditions for the community as well as efforts to reduce the influence of the country’s founding document, the Treaty of Waitangi, on policy.

(Reporting by Alasdair Pal and Lucy Craymer in Wellington; Editing by Saad Sayeed and Hugh Lawson)

By Lucy Craymer and Alasdair Pal WELLINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) – New Zealand’s ruling centre-right National Party and main opposition Labour were running neck and neck as counting began in the nationwide general election, but early projections showed the incumbent coalition would win enough seats to retain power.

Results from the Electoral Commission show that with 14.4% of the results counted, the National Party has 30.90% of the party vote, with the centre-left Labour on 28.39% of the vote.

A seat projection from New Zealand’s Electoral Commission showed the current three-party ruling coalition led by National was heading toward remaining in control after an election dominated by a struggling economy and voter disillusionment with the two biggest contenders.

Show Full Article

“I think the (National Party) are a bit higher than we expected in complete honesty with you,” Labour lawmaker Kieran McNulty said in an interview with public broadcaster TVNZ.

“We’re not reading too much into it because it’s a relatively low level of votes that have been declared.”

Left-leaning parties including Labour are aiming to make the National Party coalition the first one-term government in nearly 50 years.

GOVERNMENT COULD TAKE WEEKS

While the Electoral Commission expects to report preliminary results from 50% of voting places by 10 p.m. (0900 GMT), there may be no new government until after official results are released on November 27 and coalition negotiations are concluded.

New Zealand’s electoral system makes coalitions the norm, and the tightness of this year’s race means one or more of the country’s smaller parties will almost certainly participate in a governing coalition.

The country switched to a mixed member proportional system in 1996, which means people vote for both the party and a local constituency candidate.

There are 71 constituency seats and at least 49 party seats and a party or coalition needs a majority to form a government.

Special votes, which include those from overseas voters or people outside their electorate, will not be included in the vote count until November 27. Historically, special votes have favoured the left, with parties on the right losing support following the count.

New Zealand has emerged only slowly from a prolonged economic downturn, with growth subdued, household budgets strained and unemployment rising to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest level in 11 years.

(Reporting by Alasdair Pal and Lucy Craymer in Wellington; Editing by Saad Sayeed)
